summary: Describes how RSVP-TE graceful restart works in MPLS traffic-engineered networks. It builds on the RSVP Hello message, which establishes and maintains neighbor relationships between routers, so that a router can restart without disrupting traffic passing through it.

plainLanguage.summary: If a worker steps out briefly, the team keeps going and the worker rejoins without everything being redone. This note explains how a router can restart while data keeps flowing.

subtitle: How routers can restart without disrupting traffic they are forwarding.

tldr.problem: When a router restarts, it loses track of all the traffic-engineered paths (LSPs) passing through it. Neighboring routers then tear down those LSPs, disrupting service. Operators need a way for a router to restart and recover its state without losing traffic.
tldr.mechanism: Graceful restart uses existing RSVP signaling extensions: Hello messages establish which neighbors support recovery, Recovery_Label objects carry labels known to the peer, and RecoveryPath messages let downstream neighbors send back the path information the restarting router lost. A restarting router waits for neighbors to help it rebuild state instead of immediately removing itself from LSPs.
tldr.outcome: Routers can restart and recover their full state from neighbors without LSP disruption. The document clarifies procedures for complex scenarios where multiple adjacent routers restart in different orders.

sections.title: Graceful Restart for Traffic-Engineered Networks
sections.content:
In MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) networks, routers use RSVP-TE (RSVP with Traffic Engineering extensions) to set up and maintain LSPs (Label Switched Paths)—dedicated routes for traffic with specific requirements. These paths are signaled hop-by-hop: the ingress router sends a Path message downstream to reserve labels and resources, and the egress router responds with Resv messages back upstream.

When a router restarts, it loses all knowledge of the LSPs passing through it. Without recovery, its neighbors would tear down all affected LSPs, causing traffic disruption and requiring them all to be re-signaled—a slow and disruptive process. Graceful restart allows a restarting router to recover its state from its neighbors instead. The router signals to neighbors using Hello messages that it supports recovery, then waits for neighbors to send back the path and label information the router lost, allowing it to reconstruct the LSP state and resume forwarding without disruption.

This document provides an informational clarification of graceful restart procedures when multiple adjacent routers restart, such as after a line-card failure affecting both sides of a link, or during network maintenance. It does not define new mechanisms; all procedures are already defined in RFC 3473 (GMPLS extensions) and RFC 5063 (RSVP-TE extensions for RecoveryPath).
sections.plainLanguage: When a router restarts, it asks its neighbors, "I forgot the paths I was handling—can you remind me?" The neighbors send back a summary of what the router was doing, so it can pick up right away without dropping the traffic.

sections.title: Graceful Restart Mechanisms
sections.content:
Graceful restart depends on three protocol extensions already defined in earlier RFCs:

Hello Messages and Restart_Cap Object. Routers exchange RSVP Hello messages to establish adjacencies and maintain neighbor relationships. The Hello message was extended with a Restart_Cap (Restart Capability) object to advertise that a router supports graceful restart. When a router restarts, it sends a Hello message indicating recovery is supported, signaling to neighbors that they should expect a state recovery conversation rather than a teardown.

Recovery_Label Object. Neighbors that understand graceful restart send back Path messages carrying a Recovery_Label object. This label is the label that the peer previously allocated on the downstream interface of the restarting router (the label the peer sent in a Resv message before the restart). The restarting router receives this label and knows: "this is the label my downstream neighbor uses for this path, so I can bind it to the correct forwarding entry."

RecoveryPath Message. RFC 5063 introduced a new RecoveryPath message sent by the downstream neighbor of a restarting router. This message carries a copy of the last Path message the neighbor received, including the upstream interface, labels, and explicit route information. The restarting router uses this to reconstruct downstream state, allowing full state recovery in both directions.
sections.plainLanguage: Three tools help: Hello says "I can recover," Recovery_Label says "you used this label for me," and RecoveryPath says "here's everything you were doing downstream."

sections.title: Multiple Node Restart Scenarios
sections.content:
The document clarifies five scenarios when adjacent routers restart in different orders. An LSP passes through Nodes A, B, C, and D in sequence. A "normal" node is fully operational; a "restarting" node has just restarted and is recovering; a "delayed restarting" node has restarted but one of its neighbors has not yet restarted and remains unreachable.

Scenario 1: Node B (restarting) has a normal upstream neighbor (Node A) and a delayed restarting downstream neighbor (Node C). Node B recovers upstream state from Node A's Path message, but must wait for Node C to restart before recovering downstream state. If Node C does not restart within a timeout, Node B tears down the LSPs.

Scenario 2: Node C (restarting) has a delayed restarting upstream neighbor (Node B) and a normal downstream neighbor (Node D). Node C recovers downstream state from Node D's RecoveryPath message, but waits for Node B to restart before recovering upstream state.

Scenario 3: Node C (restarting) has delayed restarting neighbors both upstream (Node B) and downstream (Node D). Node C starts a recovery timer and waits for both neighbors to restart and resend state.

Scenarios 4 and 5: The restarting node is the ingress (Scenario 4, Node A with Node B delayed restarting) or egress (Scenario 5, Node D with Node C delayed restarting). In these cases, the restarting router handles recovery from the applicable direction (downstream for ingress, upstream for egress) while waiting for the neighbor to return.

In all cases, the key principle is that a restarting router maintains a recovery timer. When it restarts, it signals neighbors it is restarting. Neighbors send recovery information. Any LSP state that has not been resynchronized when the timer expires is cleared. This prevents the router from holding stale LSP state indefinitely if a neighbor never restarts.
sections.plainLanguage: Different scenarios happen depending on where the restart happens in the path (middle, one end, or both ends) and whether neighbors restart before or after the restarting router. The restarting router waits for neighbors to recover what it can, then gives up on parts it cannot recover in time.

sections.title: Implementation and State Recovery
sections.content:
The RSVP state that must be recovered consists of two main blocks: the Path State Block (PSB) containing upstream information (the interface and label received from upstream, the explicit route), and the Resv State Block (RSB) containing downstream information (the interface and label sent downstream). Some implementations combine these into a single LSP state block.

When recovering from neighbors, a restarting node retrieves its PSB from a Path message with a Recovery_Label object sent by the upstream neighbor. It retrieves its RSB from a RecoveryPath message sent by the downstream neighbor. The restarting node must reconcile recovered RSVP state with the data plane (the actual forwarding table). If data plane forwarding entries exist, they are bound to the recovered LSP state. If mismatches occur, local policy determines the action: reprogram the data plane, alert the management plane, or tear down the LSP.

The document emphasizes that these procedures do not define new processes; they clarify how existing mechanisms in RFC 3473 and RFC 5063 apply in multi-node failure scenarios. Implementers follow the normative specifications in those RFCs, and this document provides informational guidance for understanding complex cases.
sections.plainLanguage: A restarting router has two kinds of state: upstream (what it learned from above) and downstream (what it told below). It gets upstream state from the upstream neighbor and downstream state from the downstream neighbor. Then it checks the forwarding table to make sure everything matches.

sections.title: Status and Security
sections.content:
RFC 5495 is an Informational document that clarifies existing procedures. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It does not introduce new security considerations beyond those in RFC 3473 and RFC 5063. The graceful restart mechanisms themselves (Hello exchange, Recovery_Label, RecoveryPath) are protected by the same authentication and integrity mechanisms as ordinary RSVP signaling.

The document's primary contribution is clarifying how graceful restart works when multiple adjacent nodes restart in different orders, a scenario not detailed in the normative RFCs. This clarification helps implementers and network operators understand complex failure scenarios and verify that their implementations handle state recovery correctly in all cases.
sections.plainLanguage: This note explains the existing restart procedures in complex situations. It does not create new security risks beyond what RSVP already has.
